title: "Cover me"
hookLine: he runs home trembling, and Khadijah wraps him up and reminds him who he is

cards: Down the mountain he comes, his heart pounding so hard the hadith remembers it. Rough ground, loose stones, a long way home. Whatever happened up there, he has no words for it yet.
No explanation, no story. He's afraid something has happened to him. He comes into Mecca, through the door of his house, straight to Khadijah, and says it over and over.
Zammiluni, zammiluni. Cover me. Wrap me up.

teach.h: THEY WRAPPED HIM UNTIL THE FEAR LEFT.
teach.b: The hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, told by 'Aishah, says they wrapped him up until the fear left him. Just that: a blanket, and someone holding it around him. No questions yet.
Then he tells Khadijah everything, and says: I'm afraid for myself. Listen to her answer.

teach.h: NEVER. SHE LISTS HOW HE LIVES.
teach.b: Never. By Allah, Allah would never disgrace you. Then she gives her reasons, and every one is about how he treats people.
You keep up your family ties. You carry the burdens of the weak. You give to those who have nothing.
You honor your guests. You stand by people when disaster hits them. He comes home terrified that something is wrong with him, and she doesn't argue theology or explain the angel.
She reminds him who he is, from the evidence of how he's lived: Allah does not abandon a man who lives like that. The picture of a man wrapped up stays in the Qur'an itself.
Two surahs, the seventy-third and seventy-fourth, open by addressing the Prophet ﷺ as the one wrapped up, al-muzzammil, and the one enfolded in a cloak, al-muddaththir.
A hadith in Bukhari ties the second of those openings to a later day, when he came home shaken again and asked to be covered.
In this story, the first comfort comes not from a scholar or a crowd, but from a wife at home, holding a blanket and telling him who he is.

how: Muslims often quote Khadijah's words, that Allah would never disgrace one who keeps family ties and helps the weak, to encourage someone who is afraid, and honor her as the first to believe.

o: wrap me up, what he said, coming home afraid
hide me, his plea to escape his enemies
protect me, a prayer said before a journey

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: never, Allah would not disgrace you

s: the Prophet came down from the cave calm and certain
'Aishah's account says his heart was pounding, and he asked to be covered.
Khadijah's reasons were all about how he treated people
family ties, the weak, the destitute, guests, and people in disaster (Bukhari).
a surah of the Qur'an addresses the Prophet as 'the one wrapped up'

games.q: you're Khadijah. your husband comes home shaking, asking to be covered, saying he's afraid for himself. what do you do first?
o: ask him what exactly he saw.
wrap him up until the fear passes.
games.why: they wrapped him until the fear left him; then she listened, and said: never, by Allah, Allah would never disgrace you.

practice: Think of someone who's rattled right now: a scare at the doctor, a bad week, a shock they haven't told anyone about.
Skip the speech and plan the blanket first, sitting with them, a meal, a call where you just listen, then two or three true things about how they've lived that you could remind them of.
If you pray, you can ask Allah to steady them.

wordCard.voice: Cover me. Zammiluni: what he said to Khadijah when he came down from the cave, shaking, and she wrapped him up.

orig.note: Arabic: cover me, wrap me up.

carryVoice: Your line: Allah would not disgrace you. Tomorrow, Khadijah takes him to see an old man who knows the scriptures. Day eighty-seven, done.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3 (zammiluni; Khadijah's reply); 4922 (the later occasion of 74:1)
Qur'an 73:1; 74:1 (the one wrapped up; the one enfolded in a cloak)
